questions.q: What does TypeScript check in const body: NewUser = JSON.parse(rawBody);?
questions.explain: Types are erased before the code runs, and any is assignable to every type. The annotation only tells the compiler what to assume. A runtime check is the only thing that looks at the actual value.
options: That the JSON has every field of NewUser
Nothing about the data: JSON.parse returns any, and the annotation is an unchecked claim
That the fields have the right types, but not their values

questions.q: Is const body = JSON.parse(raw) as NewUser any safer than the annotation const body: NewUser = JSON.parse(raw)?
questions.explain: An assertion changes only what the compiler believes. It never converts or validates (Type assertions). Both lines compile to the same JavaScript: const body = JSON.parse(raw).
options: Yes, as throws when the shape is wrong
No, both are claims the compiler cannot check; neither looks at the data
No, the annotation is safer because it checks at runtime

questions.q: Where should an API validate a request body?
questions.explain: Validate once at the edge and pass the typed result inward. Checking again everywhere spreads the rules around (and they drift); checking only in the browser trusts clients you do not control.
options: In every function that uses the order, to be safe
Once, at the boundary where the body enters the program; inner functions take the validated type
In the browser only, before sending

questions.q: A handler validates the body, then saves { ...rawBody, status: "pending" }. What is wrong?
questions.explain: Validators that strip unknown keys return a clean copy. Using the raw input instead of that copy throws the protection away. Always continue with the parsed output.
options: It saves the raw body, so fields the validator ignored (such as role or totalKobo) are saved too: mass assignment

questions.q: What does "parse, don't validate" mean?
questions.explain: A check that returns true leaves you holding the original, untyped value. A parser returns a new value whose type proves the checks passed, so the rest of the code cannot accidentally use unchecked data.
options: Never write validation code; use JSON.parse instead
Turn untrusted input into a new, typed value (or a list of problems), and use only that value afterwards
Validate in the parser of the programming language

questions.q: A team adds phone: string to the Customer type but forgets the hand-written validator, which ends in return input as Customer. What happens?
questions.explain: The type and the checks are separate pieces of code joined by an assertion, so nothing connects them. Deriving the type from a schema (Infer, z.infer) removes the second copy that can drift.
options: tsc reports that the validator does not check phone
It compiles; at runtime customers without a phone pass validation, and code that reads customer.phone crashes
The validator starts rejecting every customer

questions.q: In the lesson's library, how does Infer<S> get the type a schema produces?
questions.explain: Each schema's TypeScript type carries what it produces (Schema<string>). infer T pattern-matches that parameter. Nothing runs; it is purely type-level.
options: It runs the schema at compile time
A conditional type with infer: S extends Schema<infer T> ? T : never reads the type parameter back out
It reads a type property stored on the schema at runtime
It asks the validator library over the network

questions.q: What does the return type Schema<{ [K in keyof Shape]: Infer<Shape[K]> }> of object(shape) do?
questions.explain: It is a mapped type: it walks the keys of the shape object and computes each field's type from its schema. That is how NewOrder gets quantity: number and priority: "normal" | "express" without anyone writing them.
options: For every key in the shape, the output type has that key, with the type produced by that key's schema
It copies the runtime values of the shape
It removes unknown keys at runtime

questions.q: In Zod, what is the difference between schema.parse(value) and schema.safeParse(value)?
questions.explain: For request handling, safeParse fits better: invalid input is an expected outcome, and the discriminated union forces you to check success before reading data.
options: parse returns the data or throws a ZodError; safeParse returns { success: true, data } or { success: false, error }

questions.q: What does z.object do with keys that are not in the schema, and how do you make them an error?
questions.explain: Stripping protects against mass assignment silently. Rejecting also tells a client that it misspelled a field (custmerEmail), which would otherwise be quietly ignored.
options: It removes them from the output; use z.strictObject to report them as unrecognized_keys
It throws; use z.looseObject to allow them

questions.q: A Zod schema turns "₦25,000.00" into 2500000 with .transform. What are z.input and z.output for the field?
questions.explain: Transforms make the accepted shape and the produced shape different. Use the input type for what clients send (and forms), the output type for what your code receives.

questions.q: A query string has ?inStock=false. Why is z.coerce.boolean() the wrong tool?
questions.explain: Coercion applies JavaScript's conversion rules, which are about truthiness, not meaning. z.stringbool() accepts "true"/"false", "yes"/"no" and similar words, and rejects anything else.
options: It uses Boolean(value), and every non-empty string, including "false", is true; z.stringbool() reads the words instead

questions.q: A form sends quantity= (empty). What does z.coerce.number().int().min(0) make of it?
questions.explain: An empty field silently becomes a valid 0. Decide explicitly whether empty means "missing" and handle it before coercing, for example by treating "" as undefined.
options: An error: empty is not a number

questions.q: Which job needs .refine rather than .transform?
questions.explain: refine adds a rule (true or false, with a message) and leaves the value unchanged. transform changes the value, and its type. Cross-field rules are refinements on the object.
options: Converting a naira string to kobo
Rejecting a booking whose check-out date is not after its check-in date

questions.q: What is the main reason Valibot uses separate functions combined with pipe instead of method chains?
questions.explain: Tree shaking removes unused modules and functions, not unused methods on a class. For a signup form on a slow phone connection, shipping five checks instead of the whole library matters.
options: Bundlers can tree-shake unused functions, so a browser app ships only the checks it uses
TypeScript cannot infer types from method chains

questions.q: Which project benefits most from Valibot over Zod?
questions.explain: Both validate equally well. On a server, bundle size is irrelevant; in a browser bundle, Valibot's tree-shakable design keeps the download small. (Zod's zod/mini addresses the same need.)
options: A Node.js API on a large server
A signup form in a mobile web app where every kilobyte of JavaScript counts

questions.q: What is JSON Schema's main advantage over Zod and Valibot?
questions.explain: A JSON document can be read by any language. The price: no type inference by itself, and custom rules beyond the standard keywords need code.
options: It runs faster in every case
It is a language-neutral standard written as JSON, so other languages, API gateways and OpenAPI documents can use the same contract
It can express any rule a function can

questions.q: You validate with Ajv and a JSON Schema file. How do you get a TypeScript type for the validated data?
questions.explain: A JSON file is data, invisible to the type checker. Some bridge is needed; the generated options avoid drift, the hand-written one reintroduces it.
options: Ajv infers it from the file automatically
Write it separately (and keep it in step), use ajv.compile<T>() as a type guard, or generate it with a tool such as json-schema-to-ts or TypeBox
JSON Schema files are TypeScript types
You do not need a type

questions.q: With useDefaults: true, Ajv validated an order without priority. Where does priority: "normal" appear?
questions.explain: validate() returns a boolean and mutates the data to add defaults (and, with removeAdditional, to remove fields). Zod and Valibot return a new object and leave the input alone.
options: In a new object that validate returns
In the original object: Ajv changed the input in place

questions.q: z.toJSONSchema turns a z.object into JSON Schema with "additionalProperties": false. Why is that not exactly the same contract?
questions.explain: Translations are close, not identical, and code-only rules like refine and transform cannot be translated at all. Know which one your server really enforces.
options: JSON Schema does not support objects
The Zod schema strips unknown keys and succeeds, while a JSON Schema validator rejects a request with extra keys
The JSON Schema accepts any value

questions.q: A schema says items has at most 100 entries. Why do you still need a request body size limit in the HTTP layer?
questions.explain: Validation happens on parsed data. Cap the raw size first (1 MB is common), then let the schema's maximums keep the parsed values reasonable.
options: You do not; the schema is enough
The schema runs after JSON.parse has read and built the whole body in memory, so a 500 MB body would already have done its damage

questions.q: A transfer request { "fromAccount": "0123456789", "amountKobo": 500000 } passes validation. What must still happen before moving money?
questions.explain: A perfectly valid account number can belong to someone else. Authorisation is a separate check, done after validation, with the typed value.
options: Check that the logged-in user is allowed to spend from that account: validation says the shape is right, not that the action is permitted

questions.q: Why should an API return every validation issue at once, each with a path?
questions.explain: Reporting one problem at a time makes clients guess and retry. Paths let a form show each message next to the right input.
options: The client can fix everything in one round trip, and a path such as items[0].quantity says exactly which field to fix
So the server can log less

questions.q: Which of these is not a boundary where runtime validation pays off?
questions.explain: Validate where data comes from outside the type checker's view: clients, other services, queues, files, old stored data. Inside your own typed code, TypeScript already guarantees the shape.
options: A response from a third-party payment API
A message read from a queue
A JSON column in your database written by an older version of the app
A value returned by a pure function in the same module, from typed arguments

questions.q: In property-based testing of a validator, why generate "near-miss" orders instead of only random JSON?
questions.explain: Random values prove the validator never crashes on garbage. Near misses exercise the actual rules: quantities around 1 and 50, e-mails with and without @, SKUs in the wrong case.
options: Random JSON almost never looks like an order, so it rarely reaches the boundary checks; near misses mix valid and invalid fields where bugs hide
Near misses are faster to generate
Random JSON is not allowed in tests

questions.q: In a ZudoJS application, which validator should request handlers use?
questions.explain: One schema library across the app means one way to read issues and one source for generated documentation. Schemas and validation in depth covers it.
options: @zudojs/schema, which the framework's HTTP layer, configuration and OpenAPI generation already use

questions.q: The annotation says quantity: number. What does this print?
questions.explain: The value is still the string "2". + joins strings ("21"); * converts to a number (6). TypeScript believed the annotation, so it could not warn about either.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The type does not mention role, but the object does, and spread copies every own property. The client's role overwrites the server's default: mass assignment.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: JSON.parse creates an ordinary own property called __proto__. Spread copies it as a plain property, but Object.assign sets it, which replaces the new object's prototype, so isAdmin appears through inheritance. Building the output from known keys, as schemas do, avoids this whole class of attack.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: These are the conversions that "coerce" validators use. An empty string becomes 0, spaces are ignored, trailing text gives NaN, and any non-empty string is truthy. Each is a trap when parsing form fields.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Both field problems are reported, not just the first. 1.5 is not an integer, which Zod 4 reports as invalid_type (expected int). The extra note is not an issue: z.object strips unknown keys silently.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: parse returns a new object built from the schema's keys: name is trimmed and role is gone. Continue with user, not with the raw body.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Coercion applies Number() and Boolean(): the empty string becomes 0 and "false" becomes true. z.stringbool() understands the word.
questions.code:
import * as z from "zod";

console.log(z.coerce.number().parse("42"), z.coerce.number().parse(""), z.coerce.boolean().parse("false"), z.stringbool().parse("false"));

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The regex checks the text, then the transform turns it into whole kobo. The output type of price is number, and z.infer reflects that.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Valibot's result has success, output and issues. Like Zod, v.object drops unknown keys; the second value has exactly one issue, the quantity below 1.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: @zudojs/schema follows the same pattern: safeParse returns { success, data } or { success, issues }, and unknown keys such as guest are stripped from the output.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Optional fields are left out of required, and z.object becomes additionalProperties: false, even though Zod itself strips unknown keys instead of rejecting them.

questions.q: Write a type guard isOrderLine(value: unknown): value is OrderLine: an object (not null, not an array) whose sku is a non-empty string and whose quantity is a whole number of at least 1.
questions.explain: Check the container first (object, not null, not array), then each field's type and value. The as Record<string, unknown> is safe right after the object check, because every property is still unknown.
questions.expected:
{"sku": "RICE-5", "quantity": 2} true
{"sku": "RICE-5", "quantity": "2"} false
[1, 2] false
null false
{"sku": "", "quantity": 1} false

questions.q: Write pickFields(input, allowed) that returns a new object with only the allowed keys that are present in the input. Use it to stop mass assignment in a profile update.
questions.explain: Iterate over the allowed keys, not the input's keys, so nothing the client adds can get through. Object.hasOwn ignores inherited properties. email is allowed but absent, so it is left out instead of being set to undefined.

questions.q: Using the lesson's schema design, write integer(min, max) returning a Schema<number> whose parse(value, path) accepts only whole numbers in range, and reports { path, message } otherwise.
questions.explain: Check the type before the range, and never convert: "3" is rejected, because a JSON body can send a real number. The path passed in by the parent schema makes the message point at the right field.

questions.q: With @zudojs/schema, define a Transfer schema: toAccount a string of exactly 10 digits (use .regex), amountKobo a whole number of at least 100. Print the issues for the bad transfer as path: message, and the data for the good one.
questions.explain: Both issues come back together, each with a path. The good transfer's memo is stripped, because the schema does not list it. Infer<typeof Transfer> would give the matching type.

questions.q: Write validateItems(items: unknown) that returns a list of issue strings like items[1].quantity: must be at least 1. Check that items is a non-empty array, and that every item has a string sku and a whole-number quantity of at least 1. Report every problem, not just the first.
questions.explain: Collecting issues instead of throwing on the first one lets the client fix everything at once. Building the path from the array index is exactly what schema libraries do for nested data.
questions.expected:
[
  'items[1].quantity: must be at least 1',
  'items[2].sku: expected a string'
]
[ 'items: must have at least 1 item' ]
[ 'items: expected an array' ]

questions.q: Write parseBooleanText(text: string): boolean | undefined for query strings: "true", "1", "yes" give true; "false", "0", "no" give false (ignore case and spaces); anything else gives undefined.
questions.explain: This reads the word, as z.stringbool() does, instead of JavaScript truthiness, where Boolean("false") is true. Returning undefined for unknown words lets the caller report an issue instead of guessing.
questions.expected:
"true" true
" No " false
"0" false
"false" false
"maybe" undefined
"" undefined

questions.q: Validators return issues with a path array. Write formatPath(path) that turns ["items", 0, "quantity"] into items[0].quantity (numbers in brackets, strings joined with dots; an empty path is (root)).
questions.explain: Zod and @zudojs/schema report paths as arrays of keys and indexes; formatting them the way JavaScript code writes property access makes messages easy to read and to map to form fields.
